title: A Biography of Earth
intro: Earth's life story in four chapters (eons): Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic, Phanerozoic. For each one, learn WHAT happened and WHY it mattered.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the Hadean Eon and the early molten Earth.
Explain how arcs and greenstone belts contributed to the growth of the first continents.
Summarize evidence for Archean rocks and early life.
Explain how cratons formed and how they contributed to the assembly of North America.
Describe Proterozoic oxygenation and the growth of large continents.
Describe evidence for major glaciations on the early Earth.
Relate Paleozoic seas, orogens, terranes, and Pangaea to changing geography.
Summarize major Paleozoic biological events, including the end-Permian extinction.
Explain how Pangaea broke apart and how western North America developed during the Mesozoic.
Describe major Mesozoic events and evidence for the age of dinosaurs.
Explain the evidence for the K?Pg impact and its consequences for life.
Relate Cenozoic continental movement to the Basin and Range, mountain building, and ice ages.
Summarize the rise and diversification of mammals during the Cenozoic.

boxes.text: Why did iron sink? Iron is much denser than rock. While Earth was molten, gravity sorted it like oil and vinegar in a jar: heavy at the bottom, light on top. That is why Earth has layers today.
Hadean sounds like Hades, the underworld: hot, molten, hellish.
Dates differ by source. The textbook says 4.5 to 4.0 Ga.

steps.title: Earth forms and melts
bullets: Hadean = **4.57 to 3.8 Ga**. It starts when Earth forms by **planetesimal accretion** (small rocks crashing together and sticking).
Three heat sources: **gravitational collapse**, impacts and **radioactive decay**. Earth got hot enough to partly melt by ~4.5 Ga.
**Chemical differentiation**: molten iron sinks to the centre (the core); the ultramafic mantle stays as a thick outer shell.

steps.title: A young sea and volcanic vents
bullets: An artist's picture of steaming volcanic vents beside a young sea.
Minerals dated 4.4 Ga show liquid water already existed.
The water may come from volcanic outgassing, comets and meteorites, possibly all three.

steps.title: The time scale column
bullets: Hadean is at the bottom (birth of Earth 4,570 Ma), then Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic on top. The Phanerozoic splits into Paleozoic (to 251 Ma), Mesozoic (to 65 Ma) and Cenozoic (to 0).
The arrow marks the **Precambrian** = Hadean + Archean + Proterozoic = everything before 542 Ma.
**Ma** = million years ago and **Ga** = billion years ago (Ka = thousand years ago).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: An artist's picture of the Hadean shows a glowing, lava-covered surface with a giant impact explosion. It shows the Hadean ingredients: a partly molten surface, volcanoes and asteroid impacts.

sections.title: Building the first continents: arcs and greenstone belts

boxes.text: Why is making the first continents a puzzle? Plate tectonics needs continents, but the easiest way to make continental rock is to melt existing continents (a chicken-and-egg problem). The answer is arcs: sinking oceanic plates feed volcanic arcs, and arcs and plateaus pile up and fuse into a larger, lighter, more felsic block.
Think of LEGO. Arcs, plateaus and rifts are the bricks, subduction is the hand that keeps pressing them together, and the greenstone belt is the seam between bricks.

steps.title: An early ocean in cross-section
bullets: A cross-section (not to scale) of an early ocean. Labelled: a **rift filled with volcanic rocks** (B), **volcanic arcs** (C and E) and an oceanic plateau (D) above a rising magma plume.
Hot-spot igneous rock will become **greenstone**; arc rock will become **granite/gneiss**.
An **island arc** is a chain of volcanoes made when an oceanic plate sinks under another oceanic plate. Several arcs can combine and eventually evolve into a continent.

steps.title: Pieces squeezed into one block
bullets: The arcs, plateau and rift pieces (A to E) are squeezed together into one block. Asthenosphere sits on both sides.
The slice of dark volcanic rock between the pieces is the **greenstone belt**. Below it, remelted crust (red) and a gneissic fabric mark where the block is cooked and remelted.
**Greenstone** is metamorphosed basalt that gets its green colour from the mineral chlorite.

sections.title: Archean Eon: first rocks, first life

boxes.text: Why do stromatolites have layers? They are fossils of photosynthetic microbial mats, so each layer is one mat of microbes stacked on the last.

steps.title: Stromatolites and microfossils
bullets: **Stromatolites** are layered mounds built by microbial mats (photosynthesising bacteria).
The small boxes in the corner show microfossils, 10 µm wide.

steps.title: Layers up close
bullets: A close-up shows the curved layers that give a stromatolite its look.
The first well-preserved fossils are stromatolites from ~3.5 Ga.

steps.title: Mounds in shallow water
bullets: Dark stromatolite mounds sit in shallow water, each one built by microbial mats.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Continents grew fastest in the Archean. About **80%** of today's continental area existed by the end of it (~2.5 Ga).

The growth curve starts near 0% at about 3.8 Ga, climbs steeply, reaches about 80% at 2.5 Ga, then flattens toward 100% through the Proterozoic and Phanerozoic. So the continents were mostly built early and then only slowly added to.

sections.title: Cratons and the assembly of North America

boxes.text: Why do cratons survive? Most tectonic activity happens around cratons rather than within them, so their ancient rock stays almost unchanged.
A continent grows like tree rings, oldest in the middle: Archean core, then 2.0 to 1.8 Ga belts, then Yavapai, Mazatzal, and finally Grenville at the edge.
Shield and platform are different parts of the same craton. Shield = exposed crystalline rock; platform = sedimentary layers on top.

steps.title: World map of geologic provinces
bullets: Legend: stretched crust, large igneous provinces, Phanerozoic orogens, basins and platforms, **Precambrian shields**, and Archean crustal remnants.
Each continent has an old core of shields and platforms ringed by younger belts.

steps.title: North America's craton
bullets: A **craton** is the stable interior of a continent, mostly formed in the Archean. It has a **shield** (crystalline basement rock at the surface) and a platform (sedimentary rock covering the shield).
The Shield (orange) is in Canada; the Western and Eastern platforms lie to its south, with Paleozoic and Mesozoic cover.
Around the craton are the Phanerozoic orogens (Cordillera and Rocky Mountains in the west, Appalachians in the east, Ouachitas in the south) and the Coastal Plain.

steps.title: How North America was assembled
bullets: Grey **Archean provinces (>2.5 Ga)** (Superior, Slave, Rae and Hearn, Wyoming) form the core.

Younger belts wrap around: Proterozoic accreted crust (2.0 to 1.8 Ga), collisional orogens including Trans-Hudson (1.9 to 1.8 Ga), **Yavapai** (1.8 to 1.7 Ga), Mazatzal (1.7 to 1.6 Ga), granite-rhyolite (1.5 to 1.3 Ga) and the **Grenville orogen** (1.3 to 1.0 Ga) on the east and south.
Pink = younger, post-Precambrian crust outside the craton edge.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **protero** = first, **zoic** = life. The name came before Archean life was discovered.

sections.title: Proterozoic Eon: oxygen and big continents

boxes.text: Why do BIFs show oxygen? Before oxygen, iron dissolved in seawater. When cyanobacteria released O2, the iron rusted out of the water as iron oxide and settled in layers. No oxygen = no rust layers. Today's steel comes from this iron.
BIF = 'Big Iron Fingerprint' of the ocean's first big oxygen event.
Rodinia vs Pannotia: both are Proterozoic. Pannotia was short-lived and formed ~600 Ma; the supercontinent that comes later in the Paleozoic is Pangaea.

steps.title: Banded iron formations
bullets: **Banded iron formations (BIFs)** are the evidence of oxygen build-up in the oceans.
The stripes are layers of iron oxide and silica.

steps.title: An Ediacara fossil
bullets: The ribbed imprint is a fossil of one of the Ediacara animals. The ruler shows its size.

steps.title: A leap in complexity
bullets: In the last 500 Ma of the Proterozoic, simple organisms gave way to complex ones.
The **Ediacara fauna** were soft-bodied, multicellular animals resembling worms and jellyfish.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **protero** = first, **zoic** = life. It was named before Archean life was discovered.
Supercontinents: **Rodinia** (~750 Ma) and **Pannotia** (formed ~600 Ma, short-lived).

boxes.text: Why did oxygen cause cooling? Free oxygen reacted with methane to make carbon dioxide. Methane traps heat better than carbon dioxide, so the greenhouse effect weakened and the planet cooled.
Ice is a bad sorter: it dumps boulders and mud together. Rivers and waves sort by size.
The 2.1 Ga and 700 Ma dates come from the textbook, and Snowball Earth is described there as controversial.

steps.title: Ice spreads over the planet
bullets: Two globes with a TIME arrow. On the later globe, ice covers more of the planet. Labels: sea ice, ice-covered land, mountains and the equator.
It fits the **Snowball Earth** hypothesis (controversial): around 700 Ma, ice spread from the poles toward the equator.
Evidence: tropical limestone found interbedded with glacial deposits. A competing idea, **Slushball Earth**, keeps some equatorial ocean open.

steps.title: Large clasts in mudstone
bullets: These strata contain **large clasts surrounded by mudstone**.
Glaciers can carry clasts of all sizes, so this mix points to glaciers.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The first glaciation, the **Huron Glaciation** (about 2.1 Ga), followed the Great Oxygenation Event.

sections.title: Paleozoic geography: seas, orogens, terranes and Pangea

boxes.text: Why did the mountains form on the east coast? When ocean basins close, the continents on either side collide and pile up mountains. Several such collisions closed the oceans between Laurentia, Baltica and Gondwana to make Pangea.
Panthalassa = 'all sea' and Pangea = 'all land'. Pan- means all.

Pannotia (Proterozoic, ~600 Ma) is not Pangea (late Paleozoic). Panthalassa is an ocean, Pangea is land. An orogen is the mountain belt; an orogeny is the event. In the late Paleozoic the east coast of North America had the high mountains and the west coast was smaller isolated volcanic highlands (Textbook 8.6.1).

steps.title: Laurentia with a shallow sea
bullets: At ~510 Ma (Cambrian-Ordovician) the continents are scattered. **Gondwana** (South America, Africa, India, Antarctica, Australia) is one big mass; Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia are separate.

**Laurentia** (the North American craton) has dry land in the interior but a shallow sea and a carbonate shelf around it, a transcontinental arch and a paleoequator crossing it. Passive margins and volcanic arcs are labelled around the edges.

steps.title: Seas rise and fall
bullets: Sea level rose and fell four times in the Paleozoic.
Each rise covered most of North America with a shallow tropical sea, recorded as limestone with fossil corals.

In the Silurian and Devonian, the oceans Iapetus, Rheic, Paleotethys and Panthalassa lay between Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia, Siberia and Kazakhstania. The **Caledonides** are the mountains where Laurentia meets Baltica; the **Taconic orogen** was a relict of an Ordovician collision.

**Antler orogeny** (Devonian to Pennsylvanian, west): a volcanic island arc accreted onto western North America, subducting away from it. In the east are the Caledonian orogen, the Acadian orogeny and the Catskill Delta.

**Terranes** are chunks of crust (island arcs, microcontinents) riding on a subducting plate that get stuck onto the edge of a continent. The map notes terranes that eventually attach to Laurentia; much of California is accreted terranes.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: In the Carboniferous and Permian the continents join into **Pangea**. Labelled on the map: the **Caledonian**, Hercynian, Alleghanian and Ouachita orogens, coal swamps and the Ancestral Rockies.

Pangea formed by island-arc accretion and continental collisions. In North America these were the Taconic, Acadian, Caledonian and Alleghanian orogenies, and the Appalachians are their eroded remnants. The ocean around Pangea was **Panthalassa**; the **Tethys Sea** later split it into Laurasia and Gondwana.

sections.title: Paleozoic Era: life explodes, then nearly dies

boxes.text: Why did animals follow plants onto land? Plants made food and shelter first, and insects ate them. Predators then followed the food.
Do not mix the units. Textbook says up to 96% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates.

steps.title: Plants, then animals, move onto land
bullets: In the Silurian and Devonian, **vascular plants** (internal veins, woody tissue, seeds) spread and formed the first forests.
The first land animals (scorpions, spiders, insects and crustaceans) followed plants onto land.

steps.title: Tiktaalik and the first amphibians
bullets: **Tiktaalik** (found 1996) was a lobe-finned fish with push-up fins and a swivel-jointed neck. It is a fossil between fish and amphibians, dated about 385 Ma.
At the end of the Devonian, the first **amphibians** appeared on land, walking on legs and breathing with lungs.

steps.title: Five mass extinctions
bullets: This graph counts **families** of marine animals with hard skeletons through time.
The overall rise in families is interrupted by extinction events. Five arrows mark mass extinctions; the end-Ordovician one was the earliest of five.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Cambrian/Ordovician: shallow seas full of corals, trilobites, brachiopods and nautiloids. In the Carboniferous, oxygen was the highest ever, which gave the largest arthropods (the millipede *Arthropleura* was 2.5 m long).
The **Permian extinction** killed **90%** of marine species. A graph of genera through time shows the big drop at the end of the Permian (P), and the K/T mass extinction is also labelled.

sections.title: Mesozoic geography: Pangea splits and the west coast builds up

boxes.text: Why did a sea flood the middle of North America? Shallow subduction of a young, hot, light Farallon plate downwarped the interior. Sea level was also high from fast spreading, warmth and melted ice.
Sevier = thin (shallow faults, 'S for stacks of slices'). Laramide = thick-skinned, deep rock, big Rockies bulges.

steps.title: The Late Cretaceous west coast
bullets: Legend: **convergent boundary**, **thrust fault**, volcanic arc. Labels: Trench, Sierran arc, Sevier fold-thrust belt, Western Interior Seaway, Coastal plain. The inset shows an accretionary prism, then the Sierran arc, then the Sevier belt. In the early Cretaceous, several island arcs collided with western North America.
The **Cretaceous Interior Seaway** ran from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic and split North America into **Laramidia** (west) and Appalachia (east) for about 25 million years.
Coal in Utah and Wyoming formed in swamps along its shores.

steps.title: Magnetic polarity time scale
bullets: Black and white bands show the two magnetic polarities, with chrons Brunhes, Matuyama, Gauss and Gilbert and named subchrons.
Magnetic reversals are swaps of Earth's poles. They are used to correlate rocks.
A caption says the rate of convection in the outer core determines, in significant part, what kind of rocks are deposited on the continents.

steps.title: A Cretaceous world map
bullets: Light blue shows shallow seas flooding parts of the continents.

At 70 Ma the Atlantic is open with a **ridge axis** and **transform faults**. There are subduction zones along the west of the Americas and the north of the Tethys Ocean, and India is south of the equator.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Pangea has started splitting in the Late Jurassic (~150 Ma). A **mid-ocean ridge** opens between North America and Africa/South America, with trenches on other edges. Breakup began ~210 Ma in the Late Triassic: the Atlantic opened first in the middle, then the south, and last the north.

Eocene map: a red line marks the **eastern limit of Laramide** and a yellow line the **eastern limit of Sevier**, with the Canadian Rockies, Wyoming fold-thrust belt and US Rocky Mountains. Sevier (Cretaceous) was a thin-skinned fold-thrust belt; Laramide (early Cenozoic) was thick-skinned.

boxes.text: Why did flowering plants spread fast? They make seeds quickly and use insects to carry pollen, so they reproduce faster than plants relying on wind.

steps.title: Triassic and Jurassic dinosaurs
bullets: A Triassic-Jurassic scene with long-necked and plated dinosaurs and a flying pterosaur.
Dinosaurs were small in the Triassic and became truly massive in the Jurassic. The end-Triassic extinction helped them and mammals rise.
Mammals stayed small and mostly nocturnal.

steps.title: Cretaceous seas and plants
bullets: Modern fish, aquatic reptiles and giant turtles filled the seas.
**Angiosperms** (flowering plants) appeared and spread rapidly, and hardwood trees proliferated.

steps.title: Dinosaurs, pterosaurs and early birds
bullets: Dinosaurs lived in nearly every environment. Trackways show herds of grazing dinosaurs on the plains, and large carnivores fed on them.
Pterosaurs soared overhead, birds began to diversify, and mammals got larger brains and specialised teeth.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: An impact at ~66 Ma on the Yucatan peninsula ended the Mesozoic (see the K-Pg section).

boxes.text: Why was the crater hard to find? It is partly underwater and partly covered by dense forest on the Yucatan Peninsula, so it only showed up in geophysical data. An iridium layer worldwide points to a space rock because iridium is rare in Earth's crust.
Iridium = 'I came from space'.
K-T and K-Pg are the same boundary (Tertiary was renamed Paleogene). Birds descend from dinosaurs, so 'all the dinosaurs' means the non-bird dinosaurs.

bullets: An artist's picture of the impact. The globe 'Earth at 66 Ma' marks the strike location near the Gulf of Mexico.
The extinction was likely caused by a large **bolide** that hit 66 Ma.
90% of plankton species, 75% of plant species and all the dinosaurs went extinct.

steps.title: Where it hit
bullets: A satellite view of the Gulf of Mexico. The circle on the Yucatan Peninsula shows where the crater lies.

steps.title: The buried crater
bullets: A colour map of a ring-shaped structure at about 20 to 22 N, 89 to 90 W. The picture has no caption; the ring is presumably the buried **Chicxulub crater**.
**Chicxulub crater**: about 180 km wide, the third largest confirmed on Earth, confirmed in 1991 using petroleum-company geophysical data.
Granite in the peak ring shows the impact lifted deep basement rock.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Evidence of an impact: **iridium** (rare on Earth, common in meteorites) in a worldwide layer at the K-T boundary, melted rock spheres, **shocked quartz**, a fern-rich layer after fires, and tsunami deposits from Texas to Alabama inferred as a 2 km tsunami.
Other possible contributors: falling sea level and the **Deccan Traps** flood basalts in India (over 1.3 million km3).

sections.title: Cenozoic geography: moving continents, Basin and Range, ice ages

boxes.text: Why does the Alpine-Himalayan belt exist? Continents that were moving north ran into Eurasia, and collisions pile up mountains where the ocean between them closed.
Basin and Range = stretched pizza dough: pull the crust apart east-west and it breaks into tilted blocks (ranges) and drops (basins).
Laramide = squeezing and uplift (compression, thick-skinned). Basin and Range = stretching (extension). Both are in the western US but are opposite stresses.

steps.title: Plates moving today
bullets: The world today, with **arrows showing plate movement** and **present-day mountain belts** (Alpine-Himalayan, Cordilleran, Andean). The inset says the southern continents were moving north at 50 Ma.
The **Tethys Sea** closed as Africa and India hit Eurasia, building the Alps, Zagros and Himalaya. The Himalaya collision began about 57 Ma and continues today.

steps.title: The western US
bullets: Labelled: **Sierra Nevada batholith**, **Basin and Range**, Colorado Plateau, Rio Grande Rift, Snake River Plain, Yellowstone hot spot, and arrows for the opening direction. The cross-section shows tilted fault blocks in the Basin and Range.

The subduction zone consumed the ridge, so the west coast changed to a **transform boundary** (San Andreas). As it grew, east-west **extension** spread across the western US and made the Basin and Range.

steps.title: Ice-age coastline
bullets: Red lines show the **ice-age coastline**, far out from today's. The inset shows the Bering Strait land bridge between Siberia and Alaska.
Sea level fell **more than 100 m**, exposing shelves as land bridges for human and animal migrations. The Quaternary ice age began about 2.58 Ma.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: During the ice age, a continental glacier covered much of the north. The **Bering Strait was a land bridge**, **New York City was under ice**, sea ice surrounded Iceland, and large lakes formed in the Basin and Range Province.

boxes.text: Why did land bridges appear? Ice sheets locked up ocean water, so sea level fell and shallow shelves became dry land.

steps.title: Life recovers after K-Pg
bullets: After the **K-Pg boundary**, plant life recovered and forests of angiosperms and gymnosperms reappeared. The first grasses appeared in the middle Cenozoic.
Birds (descendants of dinosaurs) diversified and spread everywhere.

steps.title: The Age of Mammals
bullets: Mammals diversified to fill the empty niches after the extinction. By the middle Cenozoic they had spread everywhere.
Many giant mammals (mammoths, mastodons, ground sloths) died off ~10 ka, possibly from human hunting.

steps.title: Primates to humans
bullets: Ape-like primates diversified in the Miocene (~20 Ma). The first human-like primate appeared ~4 Ma. The genus *Homo* appeared 2.4 Ma.
Later: *H. erectus* ~1.6 Ma (could make stone axes), *H. sapiens* ~500 ka, modern humans ~190 ka.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Ice ages dropped sea level by more than **100 m**, exposing land bridges.

boxes.text: These three questions summarize the topic: oxygen gave us iron ore, the Archean made the crust, and subduction was the likely machine.
Hot spots make oceanic plateaus and greenstone, not most of the continental crust.

steps.title: Where did car steel iron come from?
bullets: Question: 'The iron in the steel in my car was probably deposited during an ______?'
Answer **D, ocean oxygenation event**. Banded iron formations formed when oxygen rusted iron out of seawater.

steps.title: When did continents form?
bullets: Question: 'The continental crust was mostly extracted from the mantle during the ______?'
Answer **B, Archean**. The growth curve reaches about 80% by 2.5 Ga.

steps.title: How was continental crust made?
bullets: Best answer **C, subduction zones**, which build volcanic arcs that grow into continents.

quiz.q: The iron in the steel in a car was probably deposited during a(n) ______?
quiz.why: Dissolved iron rusted out of the ocean when oxygen appeared, forming banded iron formations, the main source of iron ore.

quiz.q: The continental crust was mostly extracted from the mantle during the ______?
quiz.why: A graph of continental growth shows about 80% of present continental area already existed by the end of the Archean.

quiz.q: The continental crust may have been mostly extracted from the mantle by ______?
quiz.why: Water-rich subduction melts mantle rock into felsic magma, which builds island arcs that merge into continents.

quiz.q: Which statements about the Hadean Eon are correct? I. It began with planetesimal accretion. II. Iron sank to form the core. III. Banded iron formations formed then.
quiz.why: I and II describe how Earth formed and sorted its iron. BIFs need oxygen, which built up in the Proterozoic, so III is wrong.

quiz.q: Banded iron formations are evidence for:
quiz.why: BIFs preserve evidence of oxygen build-up in the oceans.

quiz.q: Pannotia was a supercontinent that:
options: lasted for over a billion years
formed about 600 Ma and broke apart soon after
quiz.why: Pannotia was short-lived, forming ~600 Ma at the end of the Proterozoic.

quiz.q: Tiktaalik is important because it:
options: is a fossil transitional between fish and amphibians
quiz.why: It was a lobe-finned fish that could do push-ups and look around on a swivel-jointed neck, a mix of fish and land traits.

quiz.q: Which statements about the Cenozoic are correct? I. It is known as the Age of Mammals. II. Glacial advances lowered sea level by more than 100 m. III. Birds are descendants of dinosaurs.
quiz.why: All three are correct: the Cenozoic is the Age of Mammals, glacial advances lowered sea level by more than 100 m, and birds descend from dinosaurs.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Land bridges between continents appeared during glacial advances because:
options: ice locked up water so sea level fell
quiz.why: Water trapped as ice lowers sea level, exposing shallow continental shelves as dry land.

quiz.q: The Permian extinction eradicated about what share of marine species?
quiz.why: The Permian extinction wiped out about 90% of marine species.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT labelled on a cross-section of an early ocean showing arcs, a plateau and a rift?
quiz.why: The cross-section labels volcanic arcs, an oceanic plateau, a rift, lithospheric mantle, oceanic crust, magma and sediment, but no mid-ocean ridge.

quiz.q: Reasoning: On a map of the assembly of North America, the crust gets younger moving out from the Archean core. What does this tell you about how the continent grew?
options: It formed all at once from a single magma ocean at 4.5 Ga.
It grew by repeated meteorite impacts in its centre.
It grew by adding younger crust around an older Archean core.
Sea-floor spreading split the Archean core apart.
quiz.why: The legend shows Archean provinces (>2.5 Ga) in the middle and belts of 2.0 to 1.0 Ga added toward the edge, so the continent grew outward by accretion.

quiz.q: Which statements about a craton are correct? I. It has a shield and a platform. II. The shield is crystalline basement rock near the surface. III. The platform is sedimentary rock covering the shield.
quiz.why: All three are correct: a craton has a shield of exposed crystalline basement and a platform of sedimentary rock covering it.

quiz.q: Strata contain large clasts surrounded by mudstone. This suggests deposition by:
options: a quiet deep ocean with no currents
glaciers, which carry clasts of all sizes
quiz.why: Glaciers can carry clasts of all sizes, so big clasts in fine mud point to glaciers.

quiz.q: Which statement about Paleozoic geography is INCORRECT?
options: The Antler orogeny accreted a volcanic island arc onto the east coast of North America.
The Taconic orogen was a relict of an Ordovician collision.
Shallow seas repeatedly covered much of North America.
Pangea was assembled by the late Paleozoic.
Coal swamps existed in the Carboniferous.
quiz.why: The Antler orogeny was on the west coast. The east coast had the Taconic, Acadian, Caledonian and Alleghanian orogenies.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Marine limestone with fossil corals is found in the middle of North America. This most likely records:
options: a rise in sea level that flooded the continent with a shallow tropical sea
quiz.why: Paleozoic sea-level rises put shallow tropical seas over North America, recorded as limestone with fossil corals.

quiz.q: Which statements are correct? I. Pangea was completed by the late Paleozoic. II. The Tethys Sea eventually divided Pangea into Laurasia and Gondwana. III. Pangea was surrounded by the Tethys Ocean.
quiz.why: I and II are correct. Pangea was surrounded by Panthalassa, while the Tethys was a bay cut into it, so III is wrong.

quiz.q: A map shows a trench, the Sierran arc and the Sevier fold-thrust belt. What does this tell you about the western margin of North America in the Cretaceous?
options: a passive margin with no volcanism
a transform boundary like the San Andreas
a rift opening a new ocean
quiz.why: A trench with a volcanic arc and a thrust belt is a subduction setting, and the map legend marks the boundary as convergent.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Why did a shallow sea (the Western Interior Seaway) flood the middle of North America in the Cretaceous?
options: Sea level was high and shallow subduction of the Farallon plate downwarped the interior.
A giant impact dug a basin.
Glaciers melted at the end of the Cenozoic ice age.
quiz.why: Shallow subduction downwarped central North America and high sea levels let the sea flood it.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT evidence linking the K-Pg extinction to an impact?
options: banded iron formations laid down at the boundary
a crater about 180 km wide on the Yucatan Peninsula
quiz.why: Banded iron formations record ocean oxygenation in the Proterozoic. The other four are all impact evidence.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Why was the Chicxulub crater hard to find?
options: It is only about 18 m wide.
It is partly underwater and hidden under dense forest, so geophysical data were needed.
quiz.why: The crater is about 180 km wide but partly underwater and obscured by forest, so it was confirmed in 1991 using petroleum-company geophysical data.

quiz.q: Which statements about Cenozoic geography are correct? I. At 50 Ma the southern continents were moving north. II. Closing the Tethys Sea built mountain belts such as the Alps and Himalaya. III. The Himalaya collision began about 57 Ma and continues today.
quiz.why: All three are correct: the southern continents were moving north at 50 Ma, closing the Tethys Sea built the Alps and Himalaya, and the Himalaya collision began about 57 Ma and continues today.

quiz.q: Reasoning: The Basin and Range province of the western US formed mainly because:
options: east-west stretching spread across the west after the subduction zone became the San Andreas transform
a large impact stretched the crust
quiz.why: As the San Andreas grew, east-west extension spread over the western US and made the Basin and Range. Laramide was compression, not stretching.

quiz.q: A geologist finds abundant coal deposits in younger rocks but none in known Proterozoic rocks. Which evolutionary change best explains this pattern?
options: Large land plants that supplied much of the material for coal had not yet evolved.
The Proterozoic had no sedimentary basins or buried organic matter of any kind.
Coal can form only after dinosaurs evolve.
All Proterozoic rocks have been destroyed worldwide.
Earth's continents were entirely beneath the ocean throughout the Proterozoic.
quiz.why: Most coal forms from abundant terrestrial plant material buried in wet environments. Large land plants and forests evolved later, so their absence helps explain why coal seams are not found in Proterozoic rocks.

cards.back: Earth's first eon, 4.57 to 3.8 Ga. It begins when Earth forms by planetesimal accretion.
Small bodies (planetesimals) collide and stick together to build up a planet.
cards.short: Small bodies stick together to build Earth

cards.back: In molten Earth, gravity pulled iron to the centre. The ultramafic mantle stayed as a thick outer shell.
cards.short: Iron sinks to the core; mantle stays outside

cards.back: Gravitational collapse, impacts, and radioactive decay.
The eon after the Hadean, ending 2.5 Ga. Most of today's continental area grew during it (about 80% by the end).
A layered mound made by microbial mats. Earliest well-preserved fossils, ~3.5 Ga.
cards.short: Layered mound built by microbial mats

cards.back: protero = first, zoic = life. Runs 2.5 Ga to 542 Ma.
Layers of iron oxide and silica that preserve evidence of oxygen build-up in the oceans.
A Proterozoic supercontinent, shown at about 750 Ma.
A short-lived supercontinent that formed about 600 Ma and broke apart soon after.
Soft-bodied, multicellular invertebrates resembling worms and jellyfish, at the end of the Proterozoic.
The eon from 542 Ma to today. Name means 'visible life'.
Plants with internal veins to move water, woody tissue, and seeds. They formed the first forests (Silurian-Devonian).
cards.short: Plants with veins, wood and seeds

cards.back: A lobe-finned fish with push-up fins and a swivel neck, found in 1996. Transitional between fish and amphibians.
Ended the Paleozoic and wiped out 90% of marine species.
Flowering plants. They make seeds quickly and use insects for pollination. Spread in the Cretaceous.
Marks the end-Cretaceous mass extinction ~66 Ma, linked to an impact on the Yucatan peninsula (Chicxulub).
Known as the Age of Mammals. Mammals diversified to fill niches left empty after the K-Pg extinction.
Dropped more than 100 m because water was trapped as ice, creating land bridges.
The first members of the human genus appeared about 2.4 Ma.
Appeared ~1.6 Ma and could make stone axes.
Appeared ~500 ka. Modern humans appeared ~190 ka.
The stable interior of a continent, mostly formed in the Archean. It has a shield (crystalline basement) and a platform (sedimentary cover).
One thousand, one million, and one billion years ago.
Modern fish, aquatic reptiles, giant turtles, flowering plants, dinosaurs in nearly every environment, soaring pterosaurs, diversifying birds, and mammals with bigger brains.
A belt of dark metamorphosed volcanic rock (greenstone = metamorphosed basalt) squeezed between arcs and plateaus as an early continent assembled.
cards.short: Squeezed dark volcanic rock in early continents

cards.back: A chain of volcanoes formed where an oceanic plate subducts under another oceanic plate. Several arcs can combine into a continent.
cards.short: Volcano chain above subduction; builds continents

cards.back: Shield = crystalline basement rock at the surface. Platform = sedimentary rock covering the shield. Both are parts of a craton.
An Archean core (>2.5 Ga) was ringed by younger belts: 2.0-1.8 Ga, Yavapai 1.8-1.7, Mazatzal 1.7-1.6, granite-rhyolite 1.5-1.3, and Grenville 1.3-1.0 Ga at the edge.
cards.short: Old core, younger belts added outward

cards.back: Strata with big clasts surrounded by mudstone point to glaciers, which can carry clasts of all sizes.
cards.short: Glacier deposit: all clast sizes mixed

cards.back: A mountain belt on the east of Laurentia, a relict of an Ordovician collision.
A volcanic island arc accreted onto western North America, Devonian to Pennsylvanian, subducting away from North America.
cards.short: Island arc added to western North America

cards.back: Pieces of crust, such as island arcs, that later attach to a continent, as in 'Terranes that eventually attach to Laurentia'.
cards.short: Crust chunks that later stick to a continent

cards.back: All major continents grouped as one by the late Paleozoic, ringed by Panthalassa. The Tethys Sea later split it into Laurasia and Gondwana.
Huge forests and swamps of the Carboniferous became the coal that powered the Industrial Revolution.
A Cretaceous shallow sea from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic. It split North America into Laramidia and Appalachia.
The K-Pg impact crater under the Yucatan Peninsula, about 180 km wide, confirmed in 1991 with geophysical data.
A rare-on-Earth element found worldwide in the K-T boundary layer. It is more common in meteorites, so it is evidence of an impact.
cards.short: Rare element at K-T boundary: impact clue

cards.back: A western US province stretched east-west after the San Andreas transform grew, making tilted fault blocks.
They were moving north toward Eurasia, closing the Tethys Sea and building the Alps and Himalaya.

eons.name: Hadean
eons.note: Molten start. Earth forms, heats up, and the iron core separates.

eons.name: Archean
eons.note: First continents and microbial life. By the end, about 80% of today's continental area existed.

eons.name: Proterozoic
eons.note: Oxygen builds up, supercontinents form and break, and the first complex animals appear at the very end.

eons.name: Phanerozoic
eons.note: 'Visible life'. The time of shells, bones, forests, dinosaurs, mammals and humans. Tap an era in the bottom bar to zoom.

eras.name: Paleozoic
eras.note: Old life. Shells, fish, land plants, first land animals; ends with the Permian extinction.

eras.name: Mesozoic
eras.note: Middle life. Age of dinosaurs. Ends at the K-Pg boundary, about 65 Ma.

eras.name: Cenozoic
eras.note: Recent life. Age of Mammals, ice ages and the rise of humans.

events.title: Earth forms
events.text: Earth forms by planetesimal accretion, then heats up from gravitational collapse, impacts and radioactive decay.
events.why: Collisions and compression release heat, and radioactive atoms keep releasing it.

events.title: Earth partly melts
events.text: Hot enough to partially melt by ~4.5 Ga. Molten iron sinks to form the core; the ultramafic mantle stays as a thick shell.
events.why: Iron is denser than rock, so gravity sorts it to the centre.

events.title: Stromatolites
events.text: Layered microbial mats leave the first well-preserved fossils.

events.title: Archean ends: continents mostly grown
events.text: About 80% of today's continental area existed by this time.

events.title: Banded iron formations
events.text: Iron oxide layers record oxygen building up in the oceans.
events.why: Dissolved iron rusts out of seawater when oxygen appears. No oxygen, no rust bands.

events.title: Rodinia assembles
events.text: Continents collide to form a supercontinent. It is shown at about 750 Ma.

events.title: Rodinia breaks up
events.text: Breakup runs from about 750 to 600 Ma, making shallow seas where life could evolve.

events.title: Pannotia
events.text: A short-lived supercontinent that formed about 600 Ma and broke apart soon after.

events.title: Ediacara fauna
events.text: Soft-bodied, multicellular invertebrates resembling worms and jellyfish appear at the end of the Proterozoic.
events.why: Bodies without shells rarely fossilise, which is why Precambrian fossils are rare.

events.title: Cambrian and Ordovician seas
events.text: Corals, trilobites, brachiopods and nautiloids fill shallow seas.

events.title: End-Ordovician extinction
events.text: An ice age lowered sea level; the earliest of five mass extinctions in the fossil record.

events.title: First forests and land animals
events.text: Vascular plants (veins, wood, seeds) spread and form the first forests. Scorpions, spiders, insects and crustaceans follow onto land.
events.why: Plants came first, so animals had food and shelter on land.

events.title: Tiktaalik
events.text: A lobe-finned fish with push-up fins and a swivel neck, transitional between fish and amphibians (found 1996). The first amphibians appear at the end of the Devonian.

events.title: Pangaea assembles
events.text: All major continents are grouped together by the late Paleozoic.

events.title: Permian extinction
events.text: Ends the Paleozoic. Wipes out 90% of marine species.
events.why: Leading idea: huge Siberian Traps volcanism added greenhouse gases that disrupted climate and food chains.

events.title: End-Triassic extinction
events.text: The fourth of the major mass extinctions. It helped mammals and dinosaurs rise.

events.title: Cretaceous world
events.text: Flowering plants spread, dinosaurs live everywhere, pterosaurs fly, birds diversify, mammals get larger brains.
events.why: Flowers make seeds fast and use insects for pollination.

events.title: K-Pg impact and extinction
events.text: An impact on the Yucatan peninsula (Chicxulub crater) coincides with the extinction of the dinosaurs.

events.title: Grasses appear
events.text: First grasses in the middle Cenozoic. Plant life recovered after K-Pg and birds spread.

events.title: Ape-like primates diversify
events.text: Miocene.

events.title: First human-like primate
events.text: Appears about 4 Ma.

events.title: Quaternary ice ages
events.text: Glacial advances lock up water as ice; sea level falls more than 100 m, exposing land bridges.
events.why: Ice sheets hold ocean water, so shelves dry out.

events.title: Genus Homo
events.text: First members of the human genus.

events.title: Homo erectus
events.text: Could make stone axes.

events.title: Homo sapiens
events.text: Appears ~500 ka.

events.title: Modern humans
events.text: Appear ~190 ka.

events.title: Giant mammals die off
events.text: Mammoths, mastodons and ground sloths died off ~10 ka, possibly because of hunting by humans.
